item.title: Hidden weapons found near primary school in Overasselt
item.description:
Hidden weapons found near primary school in Overasselt

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Military police have found multiple weapons hidden near a primary school in Overassel following last week’s gun attack on a property in the Gelderland village, which resulted in the murder of one man and serious injury on two police officers.

Investigations have been ongoing since the attack, with 35 people arrested – all but two of whom are being held for murder or manslaughter – and extensive searches in the surrounding areas. It is suspected the attack was part of a feud over cocaine dealing linked with a resident of the village, who has been targetted before.

Police would not say how many weapons were found near the school or other details. In the day after the attack, dozens of men – who were seen heavily armed on CCTV footage – were caught hiding in the countryside, on the motorways and near rail stations as they fled the scene.

After the events unfolded, a video surfaced on social media of masked men holding automatic weapons and reading out a threat message to Jan G. Jr., the Overassel resident linked to the attack. They said he owed a “Belgian friend” 1,283 kilograms of “goods” and had to return it within 12 hours or they would kill his family.

They spoke in a heavy Spanish accent and said the goods had never left Spain as they were supposed to.

On Tuesday, Spanish police intercepted a shipment of exactly 1,283 kilograms of cocaine in a transport truck carrying coconuts. It is not yet clear whether the two cases are connected.

The shock of the attack on Overassel pushed justice minister David van Weel to warn that “unprecedented” violence is occurring due to international drugs smuggling, though he dismissed the idea of the Netherlands becoming a so-called “narco state”.

Reports of gunshots in nearby Nijmegen on Monday night drew in heavily armed police, who closed off several streets before determining no shots were fired. A relative of Jan G. Jr, who lives in the city, was moved for his own protection.

item.title: Five inburgering exam myths, tested against real exams
item.description:
Partner content

Five inburgering exam myths, tested against real exams

September 9, 2026

A lot of people preparing for the inburgeringsexamen run into advice: “pick the longest answer”, “choose B if you are stuck”, “expect it to get harder as you go up a level”. Most of it is passed on in good faith. Almost none of it has ever been checked. Inburgeringscursus.nl coded 881 questions from 35 official exam sets – three years of the Staatsexamen NT2 plus the DUO practice exams.

Here are the myths that came up most often:

“Pick the answer with words you recognise from the text”
This is the most repeated piece of exam advice there is and it does not hold up against the data. We checked it on 288 reading questions. In four of them there was exactly one option that shared words with the text. The rest of the time it pointed at two or three answers at once.

The reason is simple once you see it. The most common wrong answer quotes the text accurately and then answers a different question. Both the right answer and the wrong ones borrow words from the passage, roughly 86% against 95%. A feature that shows up in nearly every option cannot tell them apart.

“Answer B is more often correct”
This one looked real. Across 176 items B came up more often than chance and it held up under statistical checking. So we tested it on all the available exams and there it landed at 31.7%. That is what guessing gets you.

Even if it had been true, it would not have helped. Answering B every time scores between 10 and 19 points across the six exams we measured. The pass mark is 24. It does not pass a single one. So when in doubt, choosing “B” is not the safe bet.

“The exam gets steadily harder from A2 to B1 to B2”
Half true. The half that is wrong matters if you are planning your study time.
A2 really is a different exam from B1. But B1 and B2 do not separate cleanly. The individual exams overlap, and the gap between them is relatively small.

There are two groups here, not three steps on a ladder. Moving from B1 to B2 is a smaller jump than the label suggests. Moving from A2 to B1 is the real one.

“The reading exam is the same task from start to finish”
Not true, and this is the most useful thing we found. It applies to the Staatsexamen NT2 at B1 and B2 level.

Above every reading text sits one line of instruction. Five of them say roughly the same thing: “Answer the question”. The last one says something different: “read the question first, then find the answer in the text”.

That line appeared on the final text of every exam we looked at, 34 items out of 34, across six exams at B1 and B2. And there the answer sits almost word for word in the text 47% of the time. Everywhere else it is 9%. The exam board is telling you to stop reading and start searching.

One warning. It is not the easy section. Half-correct answers appear twice as often there, 24% against 12%. In 13 of those 34 items the information you need sits in two separate articles. The difficulty moves from understanding to locating. Searching faster without checking is how you walk into it.

“KNM is mostly about Dutch customs and etiquette”
Not really. KNM covers eight themes across 40 questions, and they are nowhere near equal in size. Work and income runs to eight or nine questions. Institutions get seven. Together they are about 40% of the exam. Manners and education get three each.

This held across all official practice exams. It tells you where to start, not where to stop. Those two themes leave 60% elsewhere, and the pass mark is well above that.

Why we counted all this
Patterns like these are only useful if you can practise them. That is what Inburgeringscursus.nl is for: an online course for the inburgeringsexamen and the Staatsexamen NT2. The platform is built on this research so you practice exactly what the real exams ask of you.

It covers all five parts at A2, B1 and B2. It starts with theory on what each part asks, then you move on to practice questions that follow the real patterns and finally the mock exams. These mock exams are timed and marked on the official criteria. The practice never runs out either. You generate new questions yourself whenever you want them, on exactly the points you keep getting wrong. This way you can practise until you know you are ready instead of hoping you are.

item.title: Intelligence watchdogs warn new spy powers threaten rule of law
item.description:
Intelligence watchdogs warn new spy powers threaten rule of law

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Independent watchdogs responsible for monitoring the Netherlands’ secret service agencies are sounding the alarm about potential new powers that would allow them to surveil citizens far more easily with far less oversight.

The plans, which were set out by defence minister Yesilgöz recently, include allowing the domestic and military (AIVD and MIVD) intelligence services to track and collect data on anyone considered a threat without gaining prior permission.

This is intended to fight “obvious adversaries” she said, referring to foreign states like Russia and China and non-state attackers conducting cyber attacks on Dutch infrastructure.

But Hugo Hillenaar, chairman of the CTIVD, which checks whether the services have acted lawfully, has said the changes could threaten the democratic rule of law itself.

Currently the AIVD and MIVD must request permission to track individuals every three months. If the proposed changes go through, they will be able to designate entire organisations as enemies. This would extend to any other body seen to be collaborating with them, like universities.

“If a university collaborates with an organisation designated as an adversary, it is no longer separately assessed whether an investigation into, for example, an employee of that university is actually necessary,” Hillenaar told broadcaster NOS.

The watchdogs are also worried about what the law calls bulk datasets: large collections of data on many people, most of whom are not under investigation. The services can get hold of them by tapping an undersea internet cable, or by buying data that hackers have stolen and put up for sale.

“Think of the data from a national health screening programme, or from the Odido hack,” Hillenaar said. “That includes information about a great many people who have nothing to do with espionage or terrorism. You should not want that data to be used without limit in investigations, or shared with foreign intelligence services.”

The bill would also let the services run AI over a bulk dataset before anyone has decided whether the services’ own staff are allowed to look at it.

“The supervisors are really sounding the alarm,” said former AIVD officer and supervisor Bert Hubert. “I have never seen them so critical and I understand very well that they are concerned about human rights.”

item.title: Non-EU doctors face €7,000 bill for Dutch medical test
item.description:
Non-EU doctors face €7,000 bill for Dutch medical test

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Doctors trained in non-EU countries will have to pay more than three times as much to sit the medical test needed to practise in the Netherlands, under a draft regulation put forward by the health ministry.

The fee for the professional competence test will rise from €1,700 to €5,371.50 in March 2027, and to the full cost of running the test – just over €7,000 – a year later, the ministry says.

People already on the waiting list will have to pay the higher fee as the price is determined by the date of the exam, not the application. Non-EU trained dentists are also seeing their fees rise by almost double to help cover government expenses for organising the tests.

The ministry justifies the cost rises by saying that they will fund more test places. Currently only 72 doctors a year can take the test, which has caused waiting lists of up to two years. There are currently no places available.

Under a new contract with universities, up to 120 people will be able to take the test in 2027, cutting the waiting times by about a year.

More than 6,000 doctors and nurses from outside the EU came to the Netherlands in the past eight years, but only about 38% of doctors and 20% of nurses obtained the papers they need to work here, according to CIBG figures obtained by Trouw. Just over a third of dentists succeeded.

Candidates must first pass a Dutch language test at academic level before they can apply for the competence test, and most then work under supervision for several months before they can register.

“The route for international doctors is tough and takes a long time,” Paul Herfs of the association for foreign-trained doctors VBGA told Trouw. While waiting, he said, they cannot work as doctors, their Dutch language skills deteriorate and they can struggle with their mental health.

The number of non-EU dentists working in the Netherlands has doubled in five years, and the cabinet said in June it wants to steer refugees with medical qualifications into care jobs faster.

item.title: Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force senate vote
item.description:
Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force senate vote

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet’s wealth tax reforms are in jeopardy after the farmers’ party BBB threatened to block them in the senate unless the coalition parties agree to a major overhaul.

MPs voted in favour of a new “box 3” tax on assets earlier this year, but the vote in the senate was postponed amid speculation that the centre-right coalition partners, VVD and CDA, were poised to vote against the plans in the upper house.

The cabinet wants to change the income tax system so that investors and savers are taxed on the growth of their assets each year, a system favoured by D66 and backed by VVD and CDA in the lower house.

But the two parties’ senators want to replace box 3 with a capital gains tax, which would be paid on the actual profit made from selling shares or other assets such as real estate.

Right-wing opposition parties, including the BBB and JA21, also favour this option, meaning the bill in its current form would almost certainly be voted down.

The BBB has said it will force a vote in the upper house unless finance minister Eelco Heinen withdraws the plan altogether, which would mean starting from scratch.

Withdraw or vote

“It can’t be up to the cabinet whether or not we examine a law in the Senate,” BBB senator Bart Kroon told the upper house’s finance committee. “Withdraw it or we’ll put it to the vote.”

Heinen had hoped to amend the bill as part of the current budget settlement so that it could be passed and enacted before 2028.

The finance minister has already torn up the plans once after the proposed new system attracted international criticism amid concern that investors would be forced to sell shares in order to pay tax on unrealised returns.

A new bill would not make it onto the statute book before 2029, costing the Dutch treasury an estimated €3 billion a year in lost revenue in the meantime.

The cabinet has been trying to reform the mechanism since the Supreme Court ruled in 2021 that the current system, which taxes assets based on a notional growth rate, breached European human rights laws.

Since then it has implemented a stopgap system that still taxes assets at a fictional rate but gives savers the option of declaring their actual growth rate instead. They can still pay the fictional rate if it works out lower.

item.title: Police step up campaign to stop illegal fireworks at New Year
item.description:
Police step up campaign to stop illegal fireworks at New Year

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch police say they will take a “zero tolerance” approach to illegal New Year fireworks in the first year after a ban was imposed on most types of rockets and firecrackers.

A nationwide crackdown was launched after the ban came into force on August 1, including monitoring border crossings and checking vehicles that have been used in the past to import illegal firerworks.

“One of the conditions for introducing the fireworks ban was an extensive enforcement plan,” Ko Minderhoud, national fireworks co-ordinator for the Dutch police force, told the Telegraaf.

“We have a larger team than ever ready to go and we are starting earlier.”

MPs voted to ban all fireworks apart from the lightest category, F1, which includes sparklers and Roman candles, last year following a long campaign by doctors and emergency service workers.

The annual fireworks bonanza on December 31 is the busiest night of the year for police, ambulance and fire services.

Attacks on first responders in recent years prompted centre-right parties such as VVD and CDA to change their position and accept the need for a ban, even though many voters see New Year fireworks as a national tradition.

30% have fireworks stashed

The task facing the police is a daunting one. A survey by RTL found that nearly 30% of people who regularly set off fireworks said they still have some left over from before the ban, but just 4% are willing to hand them in.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by RTL Nieuwspanel (@rtlnieuwspanel)

Just seven people turned up on the first day of an amnesty in Terneuzen on September 1 to take advantage of an offer to dispose of their fireworks anonymously without risking a fine.

The amnesty runs until October 9, with police buses touring the country to collect fireworks that are no longer permitted such as rockets and fountains.

Minderhoud said the illegal fireworks trade has been taken over in recent years by criminal gangs and increasingly resembles the drugs trade. “It’s become a sideline for classic organised criminals, because there’s a lot of money to be made,” he said.

“We see armed men transporting container loads. It was a different story a few years ago.”

He urged consumers to play their part by not buying illegal fireworks at New Year. “Set a good example and abide by the law,” he said.

“It’s also very dangerous. Look at the recent incidents at football matches. If you buy fireworks despite the ban, you’re getting involved in a murky world with very dangerous stuff.”

item.title: Two arrested after Gaza protesters spray parliament building
item.description:
Two arrested after Gaza protesters spray parliament building

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two people have been arrested after protesters sprayed “Boycot Gaza” slogans on the windows of the Dutch parliament building and interrupted the weekly ministers’ question time session.

Demonstrators twice shouted slogans from the public gallery while Geert Wilders, leader of the far-right PVV party and a staunch supporter of Israel, was speaking in parliament on Tuesday.

Access to the building was closed to visitors, but people inside were allowed to leave while some MPs slipped out via the bike parking garage.

The protest group XR Justice Now later posted a messaged on its Instagram page saying it wanted to highlight what it called Dutch “complicity” in Gaza.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by JUSTICE NOW! (@xr.justicenow)

One of the demonstrators shouted “blood on your hands” and “Free Palestine” as they were being led away during Wilders’ speech.

Parliamentary chairman Thom van Campen suspended the sitting after the second interruption and ordered the gallery to be cleared before the debate resumed.

item.title: Everyone’s tax bill is falling, except the top 10%: CBS
item.description:
Everyone’s tax bill is falling, except the top 10%: CBS

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The share of income going on income tax has fallen for all income groups over the past ten years, except for the top 10% of earners, according to the national statistics office CBS. The top tier pays 24.9% of its income in tax, while the very lowest pays nothing.

The typical household paid 12.3% of its gross income in income tax and national insurance contributions in 2024, down from 15.4% in 2011.

The figures do not include VAT, which hits the poorest hardest, or pension and unemployment insurance premiums. Including all taxes and premiums, the typical household paid 32.3% in 2024, against 35.2% in 2011.

The figures also don’t say anything about purchasing power. Consumer prices are more than a fifth higher than in 2021, and inflation was 3.3% in August, driven by rising energy costs.

Low earners
The highest earners paid 24.9% in 2024, slightly more than the 24.7% they paid in 2014. Every other group is paying less.

The biggest drop was for low earners. The second-poorest 10% of households now pay 2.3% of their income in tax, down from 6.7% in 2014. CBS said the employment tax credit was raised substantially over the period, particularly for lower incomes.

“You see a levelling trend here,” CBS chief economist Peter Hein van Mulligen told the Telegraaf. Whether income inequality has fallen as a result cannot be read from these figures alone, he said, and other CBS data show it has stayed broadly stable.

Singles pay most, self-employed more
Couples with two incomes pay far less than anyone else on the same income. On a household income of around €100,000, a couple with two salaries pays 11.9% in tax, a couple with one salary pays 19.4% and a single person pays 22.5%.

The self-employed are the only group paying more than a decade ago, up from 13.4% to 15.6%.

item.title: Freight carried by waterways drops to lowest level in 15 years
item.description:
Freight carried by waterways drops to lowest level in 15 years

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Freight traffic on Dutch waterways slumped during the summer drought as low river levels forced barge operators to take lighter loads.

Figures from the national statistics agency CBS show the amount of cargo taken by water was down by 19% in August compared to the previous year.

In the entire month 21.8 million tonnes were transported, the lowest level in August for 15 years. The average load per vessel was 1300 tonnes, the same as during the last drought in 2022, compared to 1500 tonnes at other times of the year.

The infrastructure ministry declared a water shortage in mid-July because of low rainfall and falling river levels. Sluice gates were closed in coastal areas to prevent seawater contaminating drinking water supplies, river cruises were cancelled or shortened and houseboats were left exposed on dried-up riverbeds.

The flow of water in the Rhine dropped to its lowest level ever recorded in August and while recent rains have eased the situation, the current volume of 700 cubic metres per second is well below the average for early September.

The drop in water-based cargo was most pronounced in cross-border traffic with Germany, with 39.7% less freight carried out of the Netherlands and 49.5% less coming in.

Goods transport also down by 9.5% in July, after volumes had been up by 6.3% in the first half of the year. More petrol and diesel was transported by water between January and June to offset the drop in supplies from the Middle East since the start of the conflict in Iran.

item.title: National 24-hour public transport strike begins
item.description:
National 24-hour public transport strike begins

September 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 24-hour strike has brought most public transport in the Netherlands to a halt, with no trains and buses, trams or metros stopping in any main city. Only rides to and from Schiphol airport are still running.

The FNV union organised the strike in protest at the cabinet’s planned cuts to social security, which it says will hit unemployment and disability benefits that transport workers are more likely than most to need.

NS is running no regular trains for the whole day. The only exception is the airport sprinter between Amsterdam Centraal, Schiphol and Hoofddorp, which runs four times an hour.

It is the first nationwide 24-hour public transport strike since May 2019, when unions walked out over the state pension age.

International services, including the Eurostar, ICE and Eurocity, are also not running within the Netherlands, and the regional trains to Antwerp and Aachen are cancelled.

In Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague there are no buses, trams or metros, and Rotterdam’s metro stations are closed. The ferries across the IJ behind Amsterdam Centraal are not sailing either.

Regional bus companies such as Arriva, Qbuzz and Connexxion are running a reduced service depending on how many drivers turn up for work.

Why the unions are striking
The strike is the latest in a series of actions against the cabinet’s plans to save €6.5 billion by cutting social security benefits over its four-year term, first set out in the coalition agreement between D66, VVD and CDA.

The original package included raising the state pension (AOW) age faster, halving unemployment benefit (WW) from two years to one and cutting disability benefits (WIA). The cabinet dropped the pension plan in April after it became clear it had no majority in either house of parliament.

Under the budget deal reached by the coalition parties on August 31, the cabinet has since scrapped most of the remaining cuts in an effort to win opposition support for its budget plan on September 15. The cuts to AOW are off the table and the halving of the WW has been postponed, according to details leaked to RTL Nieuws.

FNV said that is not enough, and that around 70% of the planned cuts still stand and the WW will still be halved and WIA payments still reduced, only later than planned. It wants the entire package withdrawn.

“It is unacceptable that the minority cabinet is cutting so much on social security,” FNV rail official Henri Janssen told NOS on Wednesday morning.

Janssen said he understood travellers’ frustration, but that they should direct their anger at the cabinet rather than the strikers. He did not rule out “tougher action”, including a wider strike beyond public transport, if the cuts are not dropped.
